newsitem.title: USA: Weaker data show slowing in U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: Weaker data show slowing in U.S. economy.

text.p: New-home building slumped during September while the pace of industrial expansion eased, reports showed on Thursday, confirming a slowdown in national economic activity in the late summer and fall.
Two other government reports showed a sharp pileup of unsold goods during August on the shelves of wholesalers, retailers and manufacturers and a spike in new applications for jobless pay last week.
Analysts said the avalanche of data indicated the economy lost momentum after a second-quarter surge, but remained healthy and poised to keep growing at a more restrained rate.
"After a fast sprint in the first half of the year, the economy is now in an extended pause, taking some rest and recuperation," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.
"But later this year, around Christmas time, I expect to see the economy pick up steam again," Sohn added.

The Commerce Department said building starts on new homes and apartments fell by 6 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.438 million. It was the biggest decline since a 9 percent drop in January 1995.

The Federal Reserve said production by the nation's mines, factories and utilities increased only 0.2 percent last month after a revised 0.4 percent rise in August. Businesses eased back to 83.3 percent of their maximum operating capacity in September from 83.4 percent, the Fed said.
The Fed also said growth in industrial output slowed to 4.4 percent from the second quarter's 6.7 percent surge, adding that the winding down was evident in nearly every type of activity.

The slowdown was widely predicted after gross domestic product, or GDP, boomed ahead at its fastest rate in two years during the second quarter, growing at a 4.7 percent annual rate on a wave of consumer spending. Many analysts expect GDP to grow at about half that rate in the second half.

As a result, the Commerce Department said, business inventories jumped 0.5 percent in August to a seasonally adjusted $1 trillion. That was the highest value on record since the department began tracking the data in 1982.

Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago, said higher stocks of unsold goods likely resulted from a combination of reduced consumer spending in the summer and planned additions for sale later in the year.
"There's no question the consumer took a little breather during the summer," Dederick said, "But there's nothing in any of this data that suggests we need to be negative about Christmas (spending)."

The Labour Department said Thursday that claims for unemployment pay shot up by 18,000 last week to 340,000. That was more than expected as the four-week moving average also rose to its highest level since the end of July, up 2,750 to 335,750.

Nonetheless, Sohn said, there still were "reasonably strong job markets, high levels of consumer confidence and pretty good income growth." That should mean a brisk shopping season in the period from Thanksgiving through Christmas, when much of the nation's retail-store business is done, Sohn said.

The drop in housing activity in September suggested that rising interest rates since the start of the year were finally exerting some drag on the rate-sensitive sector. But it still left starts at a healthy level, industry analysts said.

David Berson, an economist with Federal National Mortgage Association, said housing markets were underpinned by reasonably strong job growth and that was showing up in steady rises in applications for new mortgages.
"We may be starting to see some edging down in housing activity, but it is not falling off the table," Berson said.
Another factor that Sohn said was buoying economic activity was the ready availability of money to lend to both consumers and businesses for spending and investment.
Federal Reserve Gov. Lawrence Lindsey, speaking to an investment association, similarly noted that lenders were making credit available at historically low rates.
"We are awash in credit," Lindsey told the Investment Programme Association.
He also said the economy can grow faster than it has but emphasised it should occur only in a stable-price environment in which long-term planning can prosper.
"That means low inflation rates," Lindsey said.
